Malaria Detection¶

Problem Definition¶

The context:

Malaria is an infectious disease caused by Plasmodium parasites. These parasites are transmitted by mosquitos and can prove life-threatening if not properly diagnosed & treated. Traditional methods for Malaria diagnosis need time and skilled professionals.

Objectives:

Our objective is to build a Computer Vision Model in order to classify image data of red cells in two categories, Parasatized & Uninfected. This model will help to diagnose Malaria through spotting Plasmodium parasite signs. As it is a medical matter, minimising False Negative is important.

The key questions:

  • What distinguish the Uninfected & Parasitized red cells?
  • What are the key metrics ?
  • What kind of image processing method can help to improve the predictive power of the model prior to the training ?
  • Which technique or set of techniques yield the best results in term of predictions and computational efficiency?

Problem formulation:

Our aim is to distinguish uninfected red cells from parasitized one with the minimum mistake possible.

Data Description ¶

There are a total of 24,958 train and 2,600 test images (colored) that we have taken from microscopic images. These images are of the following categories:

Parasitized: The parasitized cells contain the Plasmodium parasite which causes malaria
Uninfected: The uninfected cells are free of the Plasmodium parasites

Let us load the data¶

Note:

  • You must download the dataset from the link provided on Olympus and upload the same to your Google Drive. Then unzip the folder.
In [ ]:
#Define zipfile path
datapath =  '/content/drive/MyDrive/trainings/MIT/notebook/capstone_project/cell_images.zip'
#Extract files
with zipfile.ZipFile(datapath, 'r') as zip:
  zip.extractall()

The extracted folder has different folders for train and test data will contain the different sizes of images for parasitized and uninfected cells within the respective folder name.

The size of all images must be the same and should be converted to 4D arrays so that they can be used as an input for the convolutional neural network. Also, we need to create the labels for both types of images to be able to train and test the model.

Let's do the same for the training data first and then we will use the same code for the test data as well.

In [ ]:
#Storing training and test folders path
path = '/content/cell_images'

#Defining a pixel size variable to set common size to all the images of the dataset
px_size = 64

#Create empty list to store the images
training_img_data = []
training_labels = []
test_img_data = []
test_labels = []

#Create a list with the name of the folders to loop through
directories = ['/train/', '/test/']
folders = ['/parasitized/', '/uninfected/']

#Loop through directories
for dir in directories:
  #Loop through folders
  for folder in folders:
    #Define the path of the image
    images_path = os.listdir(path + dir + folder)
    #Loop through images
    for i in images_path:
      #Open image file
      img = Image.open(path + dir + folder + i)
      #Resize image using previously set pixel size variable
      img = img.resize((px_size, px_size))
      #Convert the image to an Numpy array
      img = np.array(img)
      #Set labels and images to the correct list based on the folder's name for training dataset
      if dir == '/train/':
        training_img_data.append(img)
        if folder == '/parasitized/':
          training_labels.append(1)
        else:
          training_labels.append(0)
      #Set labels and images to the correct list based on the folder's name for test dataset
      else:
        test_img_data.append(img)
        if folder == '/parasitized/':
          test_labels.append(1)
        else:
          test_labels.append(0)

#Convert the result list to Numpy array
training_img_data = np.array(training_img_data)
test_img_data = np.array(test_img_data)
training_labels = np.array(training_labels)
test_labels = np.array(test_labels)

Plotting the mean images for parasitized and uninfected

In [ ]:
#Function to plot an image of the mean pixel values for a given category
def mean_image_plot(image_data, label):
  #Define index variable based on given category
  id = 1 if label=='Parasitized' else 0
  #Compute mean pixel values
  mean_img = np.mean(image_data[training_labels == id], axis=0)
  #Show image
  plt.imshow(mean_img)
  #Define image caption
  plt.title('Mean ' + label + ' Image')
  plt.axis('off')
  plt.show()

Model Building¶

Importing the required libraries for building and training our Model

In [ ]:
#Import libraries and modules for the ANN and CNN models
import tensorflow as tf

from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.preprocessing import MinMaxScaler
from sklearn.metrics import classification_report, confusion_matrix

from tensorflow.keras.models import Sequential
from tensorflow.keras.layers import Dense, Dropout, Activation, BatchNormalization, Flatten, Conv2D, MaxPooling2D, LeakyReLU
from tensorflow.keras.losses import categorical_crossentropy
from tensorflow.keras.optimizers import Adam
from tensorflow.keras.utils import to_categorical
from tensorflow.keras.callbacks import EarlyStopping, ModelCheckpoint

from tensorflow.keras import backend

One Hot Encoding the train and test labels

In [ ]:
training_labels = to_categorical(training_labels)
test_labels = to_categorical(test_labels)

Base model

Model architecture

In [ ]:
#Create an instance of the model
base_model = Sequential()
#First convolution layer
base_model.add(Conv2D(16, (3, 3), input_shape=(64, 64, 3), activation='relu'))
#Second convolution layer
base_model.add(Conv2D(16, (3, 3), input_shape=(64, 64, 3), activation='relu'))
#Max Pooling layer
base_model.add(MaxPooling2D(pool_size=(2, 2)))
#Reshape data for dense layer
base_model.add(Flatten())
#Dense Network
base_model.add(Dense(16, activation='relu'))
base_model.add(LeakyReLU(alpha=0.1))
base_model.add(Dense(2, activation='softmax'))

Model compiling

In [ ]:
#Compile the model
base_model.compile(optimizer=Adam(learning_rate = 0.001), loss='categorical_crossentropy', metrics=['accuracy'])

Callbacks Settings

In [ ]:
#Setting patience to 2 for fast prototyping
callbacks = [EarlyStopping(monitor = 'val_loss', patience = 2),
             ModelCheckpoint('best_model.keras', monitor = 'val_loss', save_best_only = True)]

Fit and train the Model

In [ ]:
#Print the summary
base_model.summary()
#Fit and train the model
fit_history_base_model = base_model.fit(training_img_data, training_labels, validation_split=0.2, verbose=1, epochs=20, batch_size=64, callbacks=callbacks)

Observations and insights: ____

  • The model is pretty fast to compute with average computation time around 110 seconds by epochs
  • The performance metrics are contrasted with values ranging from 91% to 94%
  • The average Recall is below 95%
  • False Negative predictions represent ~9.3% of the predictions
  • False Positive predictions represent ~6.7% of the predictions
  • The model is interesting on the computational efficiency side but lack predictive performances

So now let's try to build another model with few more add on layers and try to check if we can try to improve the model. Therefore try to build a model by adding few layers if required and altering the activation functions.

Model Architecture

In [ ]:
#Create an instance of the model
add_model1 = Sequential()
#First convolution layer
add_model1.add(Conv2D(128, (3, 3), input_shape=(64, 64, 3)))
#LeakyRelu activation
add_model1.add(LeakyReLU(alpha=0.1))
#Dropout

#Second convolution layer
add_model1.add(Conv2D(64, (3, 3)))
#LeakyRelu activation
add_model1.add(LeakyReLU(alpha=0.1))
#Third convolution layer
add_model1.add(Conv2D(32, (3, 3)))
#LeakyRelu activation
add_model1.add(LeakyReLU(alpha=0.1))
#Fourth convolution layer
add_model1.add(Conv2D(16, (3, 3)))
#LeakyRelu activation
add_model1.add(LeakyReLU(alpha=0.1))
#Fith convolution layer
add_model1.add(Conv2D(8, (3, 3)))
#LeakyRelu activation
add_model1.add(LeakyReLU(alpha=0.1))
#Max Pooling layer
add_model1.add(MaxPooling2D(pool_size=(2, 2)))

add_model1.add(Flatten())

#Dense Network

add_model1.add(Dense(32, activation='relu'))
#Second dense layer
add_model1.add(Dense(16, activation='relu'))
#Output layer
add_model1.add(Dense(2, activation='softmax'))

Observations and insights: ____

  • The model show small Dropout in validation accuracy
  • The model is pretty expensive with an average time by epoch of 1598 seconds running on CPUs
  • The performance metrics are high and balance with values around 98%
  • The Recall is high wich is a good point for medical purpose
  • False Negative predictions represent ~1.25% of the predictions
  • False Positive predictions represent ~1.95% of the predictions
  • The model could be improved on the computational cost aspect
  • Previous test on the elective notebook showed that simpler model perform well enought, starting from this model and simplify it could make it better
  • Adding more DropOut layer and/or raise DropOut percentage may help aswell
  • Reducing resolution and using HSV convertion could be a good way to decrease computational cost of the model

Model with additional Dropout layers¶

In [ ]:
#Clean memory from previous model
backend.clear_session()

Model Architecture

In [ ]:
#Create an instance of the model
add_model2 = Sequential()
#First convolution layer
add_model2.add(Conv2D(128, (3, 3), input_shape=(64, 64, 3)))
#LeakyRelu activation
add_model2.add(LeakyReLU(alpha=0.1))
#Dropout
add_model2.add(Dropout(0.3))
#Second convolution layer
add_model2.add(Conv2D(64, (3, 3)))
#LeakyRelu activation
add_model2.add(LeakyReLU(alpha=0.1))
#Dropout
add_model2.add(Dropout(0.3))
#Third convolution layer
add_model2.add(Conv2D(32, (3, 3)))
#LeakyRelu activation
add_model2.add(LeakyReLU(alpha=0.1))
#Dropout
add_model2.add(Dropout(0.2))
#Fourth convolution layer
add_model2.add(Conv2D(16, (3, 3)))
#LeakyRelu activation
add_model2.add(LeakyReLU(alpha=0.1))
#Dropout
add_model2.add(Dropout(0.2))
#Fith convolution layer
add_model2.add(Conv2D(8, (3, 3)))
#LeakyRelu activation
add_model2.add(LeakyReLU(alpha=0.1))
#Dropout
add_model2.add(Dropout(0.2))
#Max Pooling layer
add_model2.add(MaxPooling2D(pool_size=(2, 2)))
#Reshape data for dense layer
add_model2.add(Flatten())

#Dense Network
#First dense layer
add_model2.add(Dense(32, activation='relu'))
#Second dense layer
add_model2.add(Dense(16, activation='relu'))
#Output layer
add_model2.add(Dense(2, activation='softmax'))

Model compiling

In [ ]:
add_model2.compile(optimizer=Adam(learning_rate = 0.001), loss='categorical_crossentropy', metrics=['accuracy'])

Observations and insights: ____

  • The model don't have any dropouts in validation accuracy anymore
  • The model is more expensive with an average time by epoch of 1700 seconds running on CPUs
  • The performance metrics are less balances but still high with values ranging from 95% to 99%
  • The Recall is better for Uninfected data whereas the Precision is better for Parasitized data
  • False Negative predictions represent ~5% of the predictions
  • False Positive predictions represent ~0.65% of the predictions
  • Adding Dropout layers increased the computational time and decrease performances of the model which is the opposite of what is intended
  • A better approach for using Dropout could be to add them only to the Dense block of the model rather than using them into the convolution block

Observations and insights: ____

  • The model re-introdruces Dropout in validation accuracy
  • The model is more computationaly efficient with an average time by epoch of 1050 seconds running on CPUs
  • The performance metrics are high and balances with values around 98%
  • The average Recall value is 97%
  • False Negative predictions represent ~2.5% of the total predictions
  • False Positive predictions represent ~3.5% of the total predictions
  • Reducing the kernel size improved the model and reduced the computational cost
  • Previous Kernel value may have been too high regarding the Parasitized features size
  • Balancing this approach with Pooling layers may help reduce the convolution block complexity without reducing the performances

Test with enhance data with HSV conversion and lower resolution for computational efficiency¶

In [ ]:
#Storing training and test folders path
path = '/content/cell_images'

#Defining a pixel size variable to set common size to all the images of the dataset
px_size = 32

#Create empty list to store the images
train_hsv32_data = []
train_hsv32_labels = []
test_hsv32_data = []
test_hsv32_labels = []

#Create a list with the name of the folders to loop through
directories = ['/train/', '/test/']
folders = ['/parasitized/', '/uninfected/']

#Loop through directories
for dir in directories:
  #Loop through folders
  for folder in folders:
    #Define the path of the image
    images_path = os.listdir(path + dir + folder)
    #Loop through images
    for i in images_path:
      #Open image file
      img = Image.open(path + dir + folder + i)
      #Resize image using previously set pixel size variable
      img = img.resize((px_size, px_size))
      #Convert the image to an Numpy array
      img = np.array(img)

#Convert to hsv ##########################################################
      img = cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_BGR2HSV)
#Normalize the converted image ###########################################
      img = img / 255

      #Set labels and images to the correct list based on the folder's name for training dataset
      if dir == '/train/':
        train_hsv32_data.append(img)
        if folder == '/parasitized/':
          train_hsv32_labels.append(1)
        else:
          train_hsv32_labels.append(0)
      #Set labels and images to the correct list based on the folder's name for test dataset
      else:
        test_hsv32_data.append(img)
        if folder == '/parasitized/':
          test_hsv32_labels.append(1)
        else:
          test_hsv32_labels.append(0)

#Convert the result list to Numpy array
train_hsv32_data = np.array(train_hsv32_data)
test_hsv32_data = np.array(test_hsv32_data)
train_hsv32_labels = np.array(train_hsv32_labels)
test_hsv32_labels = np.array(test_hsv32_labels)

Observations and insights: ____

  • HSV converted images helps highligh the differents features present in the data
  • Reduced resolution don't seems to alter proeminent features
  • Converted image of the Parasitized data all present the same bright desaturated green spot(s)
  • Resolution decrease will most certainly help with computational cost reduction as there is less data to analyse
  • HSV conversion may help keeping the same performance if not improve them as it brings up some features that seems to be specific to a category

Model architecture¶

In [ ]:
#Clean memory from previous model
backend.clear_session()
In [ ]:
#Create an instance of the model
hsv32_model1 = Sequential()
#First convolution layer
hsv32_model1.add(Conv2D(128, (3, 3), input_shape=(32, 32, 3)))
#LeakyRelu activation
hsv32_model1.add(LeakyReLU(alpha=0.1))
#Dropout
hsv32_model1.add(Dropout(0.3))
#Second convolution layer
hsv32_model1.add(Conv2D(64, (3, 3)))
#LeakyRelu activation
hsv32_model1.add(LeakyReLU(alpha=0.1))
#Dropout
hsv32_model1.add(Dropout(0.3))
#Third convolution layer
hsv32_model1.add(Conv2D(32, (3, 3)))
#LeakyRelu activation
hsv32_model1.add(LeakyReLU(alpha=0.1))
#Dropout
hsv32_model1.add(Dropout(0.2))
#Fourth convolution layer
hsv32_model1.add(Conv2D(16, (3, 3)))
#LeakyRelu activation
hsv32_model1.add(LeakyReLU(alpha=0.1))
#Dropout
hsv32_model1.add(Dropout(0.2))
#Fith convolution layer
hsv32_model1.add(Conv2D(8, (3, 3)))
#LeakyRelu activation
hsv32_model1.add(LeakyReLU(alpha=0.1))
#Dropout
hsv32_model1.add(Dropout(0.2))
#Max Pooling layer
hsv32_model1.add(MaxPooling2D(pool_size=(2, 2)))
#Reshape data for dense layer
hsv32_model1.add(Flatten())

#Dense Network
#First dense layer
hsv32_model1.add(Dense(32, activation='relu'))
#Second dense layer
hsv32_model1.add(Dense(16, activation='relu'))
#Output layer
hsv32_model1.add(Dense(2, activation='softmax'))

  • The result of this model is encouraging for the solution with HSV conversion and resolution reduction

Simplified Convolution Block with the HSV image (32x32)¶

Previously, on the elective project, the tests made seems to aim toward the idea that increase in model complexity did not mean increase in perdiction performances. Since the model is now built using altered data and show decrease in performances, further test will rely on simplifying the model

In [ ]:
#Clean memory from previous model
backend.clear_session()
In [ ]:
#Set seed for reproductability
np.random.seed(56)
import random
random.seed(56)
tf.random.set_seed(56)

Model architecture¶

Let's modify few parameters:

  • Decrease the numbers of layer in the Convolution block
  • Increase the kernel size (to accelarate the convolution block)
  • Reduce slope of the activation function (the idea is to get rid of less valuable features in the data earlier in the training)
In [ ]:
#Modified Kernel size and less filters
#Create an instance of the model
hsv32_model2 = Sequential()
#First convolution layer
hsv32_model2.add(Conv2D(64, (4, 4), input_shape=(32, 32, 3)))
#LeakyRelu activation
hsv32_model2.add(LeakyReLU(alpha=0.02))                            #reducing LeakyRelu function slope
#Dropout
hsv32_model2.add(Dropout(0.3))
#Second convolution layer
hsv32_model2.add(Conv2D(32, (4, 4)))
#LeakyRelu activation
hsv32_model2.add(LeakyReLU(alpha=0.02))                            #reducing LeakyRelu function slope
#Dropout
hsv32_model2.add(Dropout(0.2))
#Reshape data for dense layer
hsv32_model2.add(Flatten())

#Dense Network
#First dense layer
hsv32_model2.add(Dense(64, activation='relu'))
#Dropout
hsv32_model2.add(Dropout(0.3))
#Second dense layer
hsv32_model2.add(Dense(32, activation='relu'))
#Third dense layer
hsv32_model2.add(Dense(16, activation='relu'))
#Output layer
hsv32_model2.add(Dense(2, activation='softmax'))

Observations and Conclusions drawn from the final model: _____

  • The model show Dropouts in validation accuracy before the 7th epoch
  • The model computational efficiency show massive improvement with an average time by epoch of 80 seconds running on CPUs with a peak at 140 seconds
  • The performance metrics are high and pretty balances with values above 98%
  • The average Recall is 98%
  • False Negative predictions represent ~2.3% of the predictions
  • False Positive predictions represent ~1.26% of the predictions
  • Despite the model needing more epochs to reach stability it is both computationaly efficient and balances the False prediction better.
  • Performance metrics are at or above 98% wich is good enough

Improvements that can be done:

  • Last percentage points were gained dialing down Alpha value from the LeakyRelu activation function, in the look for better model trying other activation function might help

  • Further image manipulation from the hsv converted data are to be tried as it helps with the simplification of the model while keeping performance metrics high. From the hsv converted file the features specific to the Parasatized cells are heading toward white value, meaning that those features are present in the three channels whereas the other features tend to be visible in bright red or purple color, signifying that the features are expressed in the blue and red channel. Converting image to different type, enhance the variation like described with the hsv converted data and recompose the tensor piling up grayscale images using the RGB channels migh enhance the performance furthermore and lower the False predictions, which can be of value.

Insights¶

  • Complex model can be detrimental to the intended result
  • As the image are not very complex, image conversion proove to be more efficient than simple augmentation
  • Techniques aiming at reducing the image complexity prooved to add to the model's performances
  • Techniques aiming at reducing the complexity in the way the model interpret data added to the model's performances

Refined insights:¶

  • Lowering resolution is key to the model computational efficiency, but this technique is sensitive to the data as reducing resolution might have disabled usefull features in the data
  • There's a tradeoff between categories when it come to precision and recall among the model tested
  • Reducing the Alpha value of the LeakyRelu activation function reduced the model sensitivity to diffuse features and helped to improve model performances and cost

Comparison of various techniques and their relative performance:¶

  • Original data, showing less obvious variations, such as hue or saturation, between category prooved less effective than HSV convert
  • Dropout layer setup added to the performance
  • Base architecture scored high but with a more complex one performances are even higher.
  • Resolution reduction massively increased computational efficiency
  • LeakyRelu activation method had a noticeable impact
  • Reduce Alpha value of the LeakyRelu activation function increase performances

Proposal for the final solution design:¶

A well-designed final solution should balance model performance, computational efficiency, and data suitability.

  • Lower image resolution to optimize computational efficiency, keeping in mind the trade-off with feature loss. Use statistical measures to select the optimal downsampling factor based on your image dataset's complexity.

  • Apply color space conversions (HSV conversion) and basic augmentation methods more efficiently than increasing model complexity, as these tend to add more discriminative power to simple images.

  • Lower model sensitivity to ambiguous or diffuse signals as it helps emphasize discriminative features and improves cost/performance balance for less complex images, such as data from microscopic imagery.

  • Monitor trade-offs between precision and recall. This ensures that gains in one category do not excessively sacrifice performance in another.

  • EDA can be done to define rationals for other type of infection perhaps to refine the model if intended.

Summary:¶

Preprocessing:

  • Lower image resolution using a complexity-driven guideline.
  • Convert images to HSV.
  • Apply additional selective augmentations (if needed).
  • Study relative data features size for later kernel size optimisation.

Model Architecture:

  • Employ LeakyReLU with tuned alpha (lower than default) for reduced sensitivity to weak and diffuse features.
  • Leverage Dropout for regularization.
  • Leverage kernel size reduction to enhance the model detection ability.

Training & Evalutation:

  • Test Precision, Recall for each category to monitor category-specific trade-offs.
  • Evaluate computational efficiency.
  • Iterate resolution and alpha values based on feedback from validation performance.
